chapters.title: Jaffna
lines: From Colombo the Swami travels north, to Jaffna, the chief centre of Hinduism in Ceylon.
The Hindus of Jaffna greet him with an address of welcome.
Their ancestors had come from South India more than two thousand years before, and brought their religion with them.
Under the Portuguese and the Dutch, public worship was forbidden, and temples, two far-famed shrines among them, were razed to the ground.
Yet their forefathers clung to the old faith, and now the sacred buildings are being restored.

lines.q: There are more things in the Philosophy of the Hindus than are dreamt of in the Philosophy of the West.

lines: The next evening, he lectures on Vedantism.

chapters.title: A name that lost its meaning
lines: The subject is very large and the time is short, he begins, so he will give only the salient points.
The word Hindu once meant simply the people who lived on the other side of the river Indus, in Sanskrit, the Sindhu.
The ancient Persians turned Sindhu into Hindu, and during Mohammedan rule the people took up the word themselves.
Today it covers Mohammedans, Christians, Jains, everyone who lives in India. It has lost its meaning.
Better to say Vaidikas, followers of the Vedas; or better still, Vedantists, followers of the Vedanta.

chapters.title: Seers, not authors
lines: Western scholars agree that the Vedas are the oldest of the world's sacred books.
But the Vedas are not the utterance of persons. Their date has never been fixed, and never can be.
Other religions claim authority from a Personal God, or from angels and messengers, speaking to certain persons.
Here the claim is that the Vedas are themselves the authority: the knowledge of God, without beginning and without end. Veda comes from vid, to know.
That knowledge was discovered by the Rishis. A Rishi is a Mantra-drashta, a seer of thought that already existed.

chapters.title: Two parts of the Veda
lines: The Vedas have two parts: the Karma Kanda, the work portion, and the Jnana Kanda, the knowledge portion.
The work portion holds the sacrifices, and the duties of the student, the householder and the recluse.
The knowledge portion is the Vedanta, the end of the Vedas, their gist and goal: the Upanishads.
Dualists, qualified monists, monists; Shaivites, Vaishnavites, Shaktas, Sauras, Ganapatyas: every sect must acknowledge the Upanishads.
Even the symbols of household worship, studied closely, turn out to be great ideas of the Upanishads, become part of everyday life.

chapters.title: Smritis, Puranas, Tantras
lines: Next come the Smritis, books written by particular sages. Their authority is lower.
If a Smriti contradicts the Vedanta, the Smriti is rejected.
The Smritis regulate manners and customs, so they change: one for the Satya Yuga, others for the Treta, the Dwapara, the Kali Yuga.
The principles of the Vedanta never change, because they rest on the eternal principles in man and nature.
Then the Puranas, written in the language of the people, teach philosophy through the lives of saints, kings and great men.
And the Tantras, which in places try to revive the old sacrifices.

chapters.title: Creation as projection
chapters.src: Vedantism (Jaffna); Lavoisier, Traité élémentaire de chimie (1789)
lines: The first common ground: nature, Prakriti, Maya, is without beginning.
God is eternally creating, never at rest. In the Gita, Krishna says that if he rested for one moment, this universe would be destroyed.
The right word is not creation but projection. Creation suggests something coming out of nothing.
Nature grows finer and subsides, rests, and is projected forward again, with a wave-like motion throughout eternity: the law of cycles, and Pralaya.
In seventeen eighty-nine, the chemist Antoine Lavoisier set down the conservation of mass: in a sealed vessel matter changes its form, but nothing is created and nothing is lost.
So wherever the scriptures speak of a beginning and an end, they mean the beginning and the end of one cycle.

chapters.title: Rain on every field
lines: What projects the universe? Brahman: eternal, pure, awake, almighty, all-knowing, formless and partless.
But the world is unequal and cruel. One is born happy, another unhappy; one animal tears another to pieces.
If God made it so, God would be worse than any devil man ever imagined.
The Vedanta answers: we make it so.

lines.q: There is a cloud shedding its rain on all fields alike.

lines: Only the field that is well tilled gets the good of the shower. It is not the fault of the cloud.

chapters.title: We and none else
lines: The second common ground, shared with Buddhists and Jains: life is eternal. Whatever begins in time must end in time.
The child comes into the world with the burden of an infinite past, to work out its own past deeds.
This is the law of Karma: each one of us is the maker of his own fate.

lines.q: We, we, and none else, are responsible for what we suffer.

lines: If I am unhappy, it is of my own making; and that very thing shows that I can be happy if I will.
Before the infinite will of man, even the powers of nature must bow down.

chapters.title: The Atman behind the mind
lines: We cannot understand God without understanding the soul, and the way lies inward, not through external nature.
In every man and every animal, however weak or wicked, the same soul resides. The difference is only in manifestation.
So in India the brotherhood of man becomes the brotherhood of all life, down to the little ants.

lines.q: Thus the sage, knowing that the same Lord inhabits all bodies, will worship every body as such.

lines: The mind, Manas, is not the Atman. There is the body; then the mind, the fine body, the Sukshma Sharira; and behind the mind, the Atman, the Self.
The Atman goes from birth to death with the mind, until it manifests itself to perfection, and is free.

chapters.title: Heavens that end
lines: There are heavens and hells too, but they are not eternal. A heaven is only this world on a bigger scale.
Those who do good for the sake of reward become gods for a time, like Indra. Indra is a position, not a person; there will be thousands of Indras.
King Nahusha, when he died, became Indra; and when his good Karma was spent, he fell, and was born a man again.
This earth is the Karma Bhumi, the land of work, from which liberation is reached.
What is worth having? Mukti, freedom. Even a king for twenty thousand years is a slave, while time and space work on him.
Ignorance binds. Knowledge sets the soul free, and it comes through love: love of God, and of all beings as His temples.

chapters.title: Personal and Impersonal
lines: There are two ideas of God in the scriptures.
The Personal God: creator, preserver and destroyer, the eternal Father and Mother of the universe, eternally separate from us.
And the Impersonal: not He, but It. Not knowing, not thinking, not creating, for these belong to want and bondage.
This is the Advaita. Our relation to It is that we are It. Misery is thinking ourselves separate; liberation is knowing our unity.
Only here is there a reason for ethics: the universe is one, so in hurting anyone I hurt myself, and in loving anyone I love myself.

chapters.title: Whatever you think
lines: What India needs now, he says, is not so much weeping, but a little strength.
Man stands on the glory of his own soul, which no weapon can pierce, no fire burn, no water melt, no air dry.
Before its magnitude, the suns and moons and all their systems are drops in the ocean.

lines.q: Whatever you think, that you will be.

lines: Think yourselves weak, and weak you will be. Think yourselves strong, and strong you will be.
Make your children strong from childhood. Let them learn, first of all, the glory of the soul.

chapters.title: My Ishta, your Ishta
lines: India has many sects, and the mystery is that they do not quarrel.
The Shaivite does not say the Vaishnavite will be damned. This is my path, and you have yours; at the end we come together.
Each has an Ishta, a chosen path, because different natures need different methods.

lines.q: Woe unto the world when everyone is of the same religious opinion and takes to the same path.

lines: Variety is the very soul of life.
If a temple, a symbol or an image helps you, have two hundred images if you like. But the moment you quarrel, you are going backward, towards the brutes.

chapters.title: The giddy child
lines: Caste and other institutions are not the religion. They protect the nation, and will die a natural death when they are no longer needed.
Yet the older he grows, the less he wants to curse any of them, for each embodies the experience of centuries.
Much advice from abroad is like that of a child of yesterday, destined to die the day after tomorrow.
Born like moths in the spring and dying in five minutes; coming up like bubbles, and bursting like bubbles too.
First make a society that stands through scores of centuries.

lines.q: Till then, my friend, you are only a giddy child.

chapters.title: Vyasa's order of gifts
lines: One pressing need remains. Praise be to Vyasa, the author of the Mahabharata: in this Kali Yuga there is one great work.
The hard austerities of other ages do not work now. What is needed is Dana: giving, helping others.
The highest gift is spiritual knowledge; next, secular knowledge; then the saving of life; and last, food and drink.
Talking is not religion. Parrots may talk; machines may talk nowadays.
Bring the treasures out of the closed books, and deliver them to their rightful heirs, rich and poor, in India and all over the world.
The more you help others, the more you help yourselves.

chapters.title: First learn to obey
lines: Above all, for ages there has been jealousy, even a wish for precedence in the worship of God.
Everyone wants to command, and no one wants to obey.

lines.q: First, learn to obey. The command will come by itself.

lines: Learn first to be a servant, and you will be fit to be a master.
Our ancestors did wonderful works. We too will do great deeds, so that others look back on us with blessings and pride.
From Jaffna, the Swami crosses the strait to India, to Pamban.
